title: The Part That Does Not Fit
subtitle: A Lanternweald continuation
content:
The first sign of trouble was a drip.

One drop. Then another.

It landed on the floor beneath the new Brasswatch water purifier, darkening a circle in the sawdust.

Danse heard it before I did.

He was halfway through explaining why our storage hooks should be measured from the floor rather than the top of the workbench when he stopped mid-sentence.

"Quiet."

"That's a very efficient way to end a debate."

"Jasper."

I listened.

Drip.

His face changed.

He crossed the room and knelt beside the purifier. The machine had been built from parts gathered with permission from three places: a steel housing recovered from the Commonwealth, a pipe fitting purchased from a local plumber, and a simple hand pump Fen had helped us install.

It was ugly. It worked. It had become our most useful project.

Until now.

Danse felt along the lower seam with two fingers. When he pulled them away, they were wet.

"Shut it down," he said.

I turned the valve.

Water stopped moving through the transparent inspection tube. The motor gave a tired click and fell silent.

We watched the last drop form, swell and fall.

"Could be a gasket," I said.

"Could be."

"You're doing that thing."

"What thing?"

"The thing where 'could be' means you already know exactly which terrible possibility you're entertaining."

He reached for a wrench.

"It passed inspection."

"So?"

"So I inspected it."

I understood then. Not the machine. The sentence behind it.

He had spent half his life measuring whether he deserved to be trusted by the correctness of his orders. Now he'd made a pump for people who needed water, and the pump had betrayed him.

"Then we inspect it again," I said.

Pip arrived carrying a crate of kitchen jars and stopped in the doorway.

"Why is there water on the floor?"

"New indoor fountain," I said. "Very exclusive. Only invited guests get damp boots."

Danse did not smile.

Pip set down the crate. "I brought the jars for filling."

"Not today," Danse said.

Pip's face fell.

"Is the water unsafe?"

"We have not established that it is safe."

That was the answer I needed him to give.

We put a notice on the door and fetched the ledger. Danse had recorded the part numbers, pressure tests and date of installation in handwriting so tidy it looked machine-printed. I wrote the time of the leak beside the test results.

A boy from Riverstone came to collect water and argued that the old pump had never failed.

"It also didn't filter anything," I told him.

He looked at the wet floor.

"Isn't this worse?"

"Today? Possibly."

Danse examined the fitting while I collected samples. Under the workbench the bolts lay in neat rows, each already sorted. He held the flange to the light.

"The thread is sound."

"Then why is it leaking?"

He rubbed one thumb against the metal.

"Expansion."

I looked at him.

"The Commonwealth housing was built for a different temperature range. The seal compresses when the pipe cools."

"Meaning your numbers were right yesterday and the part is wrong today."

"Meaning I should have accounted for the difference."

"Yes," I said.

He stared.

I hadn't said it to hurt him. He knew that.

"Yes," I repeated. "You should have. Now we know. It doesn't make you a fraud."

He set the flange down very carefully.

"I didn't say it did."

"You didn't have to."

For a while we worked in silence. Then Toph arrived from Riverstone Terrace with a small bag of stone wedges and absolutely no patience.

"Wow," she said, tapping a bare foot against the floor. "You can hear that pipe being miserable from the street."

Danse looked up.

"Your diagnostic terminology is imprecise."

"Your pipe is still leaking, Sparky."

He drew a long breath.

I handed Toph a dry rag before she could make things worse on purpose.

"Can you tell whether the floor support is shifting?"

"Sure. I can tell the floor hates that heavy box on one side. But I can't tell you whether your little metal ring is going to leak again tomorrow. That's your job."

Danse examined her, the distrust at the edges of his expression slowly giving way to professional interest.

"The load is uneven?"

"By enough that I'm surprised your desk hasn't written a complaint."

They argued for twenty minutes about bracing.

I found a pencil and made notes.

At the end of the argument, we'd learned three useful things. The floor had settled unevenly after rain. The gasket was the wrong material. And both specialists were better at seeing the other problem once they stopped demanding that it look like their own.

Pip watched from a stool.

"Are you two friends?" they asked.

"No," Danse and Toph said together.

I laughed hard enough to make Danse glare at me.

We ordered a replacement fitting from a local supplier. The repair would take two days. Until then, I helped Pip carry a signed notice to the square and arranged access to a safe hand pump on the other side of the yard. We checked how far people would have to walk with full containers. We adjusted the notice to mention those who could not carry them. Pip volunteered for delivery shifts, after asking who would be home.

By evening, Danse was still studying the ledger.

"You can stop," I said.

"The report is incomplete."

"The report is accurate enough to say we don't know everything yet."

He looked at me.

"I dislike that sentence."

"I've noticed."

I sat beside him. The shop smelled of metal filings and wet timber. He had taken off his work gloves, but there was a dark mark along his wrist from the strap.

"I was taught that command means responsibility," he said.

"It does."

"And when something fails, you identify who should have prevented it."

"You did identify that. You also shut it down, told people the truth, and arranged another source of water."

He rested his palms on the table.

"It still failed."

"Yes."

He turned toward me. "You're not going to tell me it's all right?"

"Not until the people waiting for water can actually use the repair."

A small, surprised smile reached his mouth.

"Good answer."

"Learned from a difficult mechanic."

He lifted my hand and kissed the knuckles. His lips were warm against skin roughened by the day's work. The touch was so careful that for a second it startled me more than any grand declaration could have.

"Do you want company tonight?" I asked.

He searched my face. "Yes. If you are free."

"I am."

He nodded once, accepting the answer as a choice.

Outside, the evening bells rang over Brasswatch Yard.

We left the broken flange on the bench, clearly marked. Not hidden, not polished into something it wasn't. Tomorrow there would be a better fitting and another test.

For tonight we washed our hands, put the ledger away and went home.
